title: Harsha’s Empire
description: An illustrated map of Harsha’s empire in 7th-century northern India, from the Pushyabhutis of Thanesar and the murder of Grahavarman, through the rescue of Rajyashri, the move to Kannauj and the defeat on the Narmada, to Xuanzang’s visit, the assemblies of Kannauj and Prayag, the Tang embassies and the empire’s end.
mapLabel: Illustrated map of Harsha’s empire, from about 600 to about 650 CE
note: Based on Banabhatta’s Harshacharita, the accounts of Xuanzang and his biographer Huili, Harsha’s copper plates and seals, the Aihole inscription and Chinese court records; each chapter says which it follows. Dates are approximate. The Vindhya forest and the Narmada battle are placed for the map, not at known sites. The map is stylised and not to scale; the areas under Powers are painted loosely and are not borders.

steps.title: The house of Pushyabhuti
steps.text: Banabhatta’s life of Harsha (Harshacharita) opens in Sthanvishvara, today’s Thanesar, a rich city in the land of Shrikantha. Bana says its royal line was founded by Pushyabhuti, a devotee of Shiva. The family’s seals name three kings before Harsha’s father, Prabhakaravardhana, who was the first of them to take the title great king of kings (maharajadhiraja).
steps.today: Today: Thanesar, beside Kurukshetra, Haryana, India.

steps.title: A sister’s marriage
steps.text: Bana says Prabhakaravardhana fought the Hunas, the king of Sindh, the Gurjaras and the lords of Gandhara, Lata and Malava. To seal an alliance in the east, he married his daughter Rajyashri to Grahavarman of the Maukharis, who ruled from Kanyakubja, today’s Kannauj. Bana describes the wedding at Thanesar in loving detail, before the bride left for her husband’s city.
steps.today: Today: Kannauj, Uttar Pradesh, on the Ganga.

steps.title: A father’s death
steps.text: Prabhakaravardhana sent his elder son Rajyavardhana north against the Hunas, and Harsha followed to hunt in the Himalayan foothills. Word came that the king was gravely ill, and Harsha rode home to find him dying. Bana says Queen Yashomati, refusing to outlive her husband, entered the fire before he died. Rajyavardhana returned in grief and spoke of renouncing the throne.
steps.today: Today: Thanesar, Haryana; the Huna campaign’s route is not recorded.

steps.title: Murder at Kannauj
steps.text: Then a messenger brought worse news. The king of Malava had killed Grahavarman, Bana says, and thrown Rajyashri into prison at Kanyakubja, her feet in iron fetters. Bana does not name him. Historians usually identify him with Devagupta, named in Harsha’s own copper plates among kings his brother defeated, and probably an ally of Gauda. Both points are debated.
steps.today: Today: Kannauj, Uttar Pradesh.

steps.title: A brother betrayed
steps.text: Rajyavardhana marched at once with ten thousand horse and, Bana says, routed the Malava army easily. Then the king of Gauda lured him with false courtesy and killed him, alone and unarmed, in his own quarters. Harsha’s copper plates agree that he died in his enemy’s house, trusting a promise. Xuanzang names the Gauda king as Shashanka.
steps.today: Today: Kannauj, Uttar Pradesh.

steps.title: Harsha takes the throne
steps.text: Harsha, the younger son, became king. His copper plates count years in his own era, which historians, following the 11th-century scholar al-Biruni, date from 606 CE. Bana says Harsha swore to clear the earth of Gaudas or else hurl himself into fire like a moth. His cousin and general Bhandi led Rajyavardhana’s army on toward Kannauj.
steps.today: Today: Thanesar, Haryana.

steps.title: An ally in the east
steps.text: On the march, an envoy named Hamsavega arrived from Bhaskaravarman, king of Kamarupa in the Brahmaputra valley. He brought a jewelled umbrella called Abhoga and an offer of lasting friendship, and Harsha accepted. Kamarupa lay beyond Gauda, so the alliance put Shashanka between two enemies. Bhaskaravarman remained Harsha’s ally for the rest of his reign.
steps.today: Today: Guwahati, Assam, is thought to stand near Pragjyotisha.

steps.title: Rajyashri in the forest
steps.text: Rajyashri had escaped her prison in the confusion and fled into the Vindhya forest. Harsha searched it with forest chiefs as guides and reached the hermitage of a Buddhist teacher, Divakaramitra. Nearby, Bana says, his sister was about to enter a fire in despair, and Harsha saved her at the last moment. Bana’s story breaks off soon after.
steps.today: Today: the Vindhya hills, Madhya Pradesh; Bana gives no exact place.

steps.title: The empty throne
steps.text: With no Maukhari heir, the nobles of Kanyakubja offered Harsha its throne, Xuanzang says. Hesitant, he consulted an image of the bodhisattva Avalokiteshvara beside the Ganga, which told him to rule but not to take the title of king. So at first he called himself prince (rajaputra) and Shiladitya. Kannauj became his capital, perhaps shared with Rajyashri.
steps.today: Today: Kannauj, Uttar Pradesh.

steps.title: Six years of war
steps.text: Xuanzang says Harsha campaigned for six years, east to west, his elephants never unharnessed and his soldiers never unhelmeted, until his army had 60,000 elephants. His claim to rule all the ‘Five Indias’ was an exaggeration. One war was with Dhruvasena II of Valabhi, who took refuge with the Gurjaras of Broach and later became Harsha’s son-in-law.
steps.today: Today: Vallabhipur, Bhavnagar district, Gujarat.

steps.title: Stopped at the Narmada
steps.text: Harsha’s push south met Pulakeshin II, the Chalukya king of Vatapi (Badami). The Aihole inscription of 634 CE says Harsha’s joy (harsha) melted away with fear as his elephants fell in battle. Xuanzang confirms that Maharashtra never submitted to Harsha. The battle was somewhere near the Narmada; its place and date, about 618 or about 630, are debated.
steps.today: Today: the Narmada, Madhya Pradesh; the battlefield is not known.

steps.title: Shashanka of Gauda
steps.text: Shashanka, the first known king of Gauda, ruled western Bengal from Karnasuvarna, and an inscription of 619 CE shows him overlord of coastal Odisha too. Xuanzang, a hostile witness, says he persecuted Buddhists and cut down the Bodhi tree at Bodh Gaya. Whether Harsha ever defeated him is unclear. After his death, probably around 625, his kingdom fell apart.
steps.today: Today: Rajbadidanga, near Murshidabad, West Bengal, is thought to be Karnasuvarna.

steps.title: Signed by the king
steps.text: A copper plate found at Banskhera, near Shahjahanpur, grants a village to two brahmins in year 22 of Harsha’s era, 628 CE. It names his ancestors, praises his brother and ends in a flowing hand: ‘my own hand, of the great king of kings, Sri Harsha’. A plate from Madhuban, dated three years later, follows the same pattern.
steps.today: Today: Banskhera, Shahjahanpur district, Uttar Pradesh.

steps.title: A pilgrim at Nalanda
steps.text: The Chinese monk Xuanzang left Chang’an in 629, crossed Central Asia and entered India from the north-west. At the great monastery of Nalanda he studied for years under its head, Shilabhadra. His biographer says Nalanda housed ten thousand monks, a figure many think too high. Xuanzang says Harsha was building a monastery there covered in brass.
steps.today: Today: the excavated ruins of Nalanda, Bihar, a World Heritage Site.

steps.title: Two kings, one monk
steps.text: Bhaskaravarman invited Xuanzang to Kamarupa. Harsha, returning from a campaign in Kongoda on the Odisha coast, demanded that the monk be sent to him. Bhaskaravarman answered that he would sooner send his own head. ‘Then send the head,’ Harsha replied. Bhaskaravarman came up the Ganga with Xuanzang, and the three met at Kajangala, near today’s Rajmahal.
steps.today: Today: Rajmahal, Sahibganj district, Jharkhand.

steps.title: The assembly at Kannauj
steps.text: At Kannauj, Harsha called an assembly to hear Xuanzang expound Mahayana Buddhism. Xuanzang’s biographer counts eighteen kings and thousands of monks and brahmins, and says no one answered Xuanzang in eighteen days. A golden Buddha was carried in procession. Then a tower caught fire, a man tried to stab Harsha, and Xuanzang says five hundred brahmins were banished.
steps.today: Today: Kannauj, Uttar Pradesh.

steps.title: Giving everything away
steps.text: Every five years, Xuanzang says, Harsha held a gathering on the sands where the Ganga meets the Yamuna. At the sixth, in 643, honouring the Buddha, the Sun and Shiva on successive days, he gave away over seventy-five days everything stored in his treasury, down to his jewels and clothes, then begged a used garment from his sister Rajyashri.
steps.today: Today: Prayagraj, Uttar Pradesh, where the Kumbh Mela gathers at the same confluence.

steps.title: A king who wrote plays
steps.text: Three Sanskrit plays carry Harsha’s name: two court comedies, Ratnavali and Priyadarshika, and Nagananda, in which a prince gives himself to the bird Garuda to save the serpents (nagas). A few medieval critics hinted that a poet wrote them; most scholars accept them as his. His court also had Bana, author of the romance Kadambari, and the poet Mayura.
steps.today: Today: Ratnavali and Nagananda are still read and staged.

steps.title: Envoys to the Tang
steps.text: In 641 Harsha sent an envoy to Emperor Taizong of the Tang dynasty in China, and Chinese missions followed, travelling by way of Tibet and Nepal. In 645 one led by Li Yibiao and Wang Xuance set up inscriptions at Vulture Peak near Rajgir and at the Mahabodhi temple in Bodh Gaya. Chinese records say Harsha received them with honour.
steps.today: Today: the Mahabodhi temple, Bodh Gaya, Bihar.

steps.title: A usurper and an envoy
steps.text: Harsha died in about 647, leaving no son. Chinese records say a minister they call Aluonashun (perhaps Arunashva) seized power and attacked Wang Xuance’s new embassy. Wang escaped to Tibet, returned with Tibetan and Nepali troops, defeated him at Tirabhukti and took him captive to Chang’an. The numbers in these accounts are disputed, and Indian sources are silent.
steps.today: Today: Tirhut, north Bihar, where the Chinese city is usually placed.

steps.title: After Harsha
steps.text: Harsha’s empire did not outlast him, but Kannauj, the city he made great, stayed the prize of northern India. Yashovarman ruled it in the 8th century, and then the Gurjara-Pratiharas, the Palas of Bengal and the Rashtrakutas of the Deccan fought over it for two centuries. Thanks to Bana and Xuanzang, Harsha remains one of India’s best-described early kings.
steps.today: Today: Kannauj, Uttar Pradesh, known for its perfume (attar).

items.name: Harsha
items.text: Younger son of Prabhakaravardhana, Harsha came to the throne after his brother’s murder and ruled northern India from Kannauj for some forty years. Bana wrote his life and Xuanzang described his court, so he is known unusually well. A Shaiva in his inscriptions, he was generous to Buddhists. Three Sanskrit plays carry his name.

items.name: Prabhakaravardhana
items.text: The first of the Pushyabhutis to call himself great king of kings, Prabhakaravardhana is praised by Bana as a lion to the Huna deer and a fever to the king of Sindh. His seals call him a devoted worshipper of the Sun. He married his daughter Rajyashri into the Maukhari house of Kannauj, and died of illness.

items.name: Rajyavardhana
items.text: Harsha’s elder brother led the campaign against the Hunas and, after their father’s death, avenged Grahavarman by routing the Malava army. He was then killed by the king of Gauda, whom Xuanzang names as Shashanka. Harsha’s copper plates call him a devout Buddhist and say he died trusting an enemy’s promise.

items.name: Rajyashri
items.text: Rajyashri married the Maukhari king Grahavarman and was imprisoned at Kanyakubja after his murder. Bana tells how she escaped into the Vindhya forest and how Harsha found her about to enter a fire. Xuanzang says she was learned in Buddhist teaching, and she sat beside her brother when he heard the pilgrim speak.

items.name: Shashanka
items.text: The first known independent king of Bengal, Shashanka ruled from Karnasuvarna and held coastal Odisha for a time. Xuanzang blames him for killing Rajyavardhana and for persecuting Buddhists. Gold coins show him as a devotee of Shiva. Harsha vowed to destroy him, but no source clearly says he did, and Shashanka probably died still a king.

items.name: Bhaskaravarman
items.text: King of Kamarupa in the Brahmaputra valley, Bhaskaravarman sought Harsha’s friendship against Gauda and kept it all his life. He hosted Xuanzang, gave him up to Harsha only under threat, and walked beside Harsha at the Kannauj assembly. His Nidhanpur copper plate was issued from a camp at Karnasuvarna, Shashanka’s old capital.

items.name: Pulakeshin II
items.text: The greatest of the Chalukyas of Badami, Pulakeshin II stopped Harsha’s advance south and took the title supreme lord (parameshvara). His court poet Ravikirti recorded the victory in the Aihole inscription of 634 CE. Xuanzang visited his kingdom and admired its soldiers. He was killed when the Pallavas took Vatapi in about 642.

items.name: Banabhatta
items.role: Court poet, author of the Harshacharita
items.text: Bana grew up in a brahmin village on the Son river and drifted with travelling companions before being called to Harsha’s court. His Harshacharita, an ornate prose life of the king, is the main source for Harsha’s rise but breaks off after the rescue of Rajyashri. His romance Kadambari, left unfinished, was completed by his son.

items.name: Xuanzang
items.text: A Chinese monk who walked to India to find Buddhist texts, Xuanzang spent over a decade there and studied at Nalanda. Harsha honoured him at the assemblies of Kannauj and Prayag. His Record of the Western Regions, and a life by his pupil Huili, are the outside view of Harsha’s India, admiring but partisan towards Buddhism.

items.name: Wang Xuance
items.text: A Tang official, Wang Xuance went to India at least three times. In 645 he helped set up inscriptions at Rajgir and Bodh Gaya. On his next mission he arrived after Harsha’s death and was attacked by the usurper, whom, Chinese records say, he defeated with troops from Tibet and Nepal. His own account survives only in fragments.
